Sources: Colorado School of Mines (left); Seth McConnell, Colorado School of Mines (top right) 3.3 Broad Conclusions on the Essential Elements for AMD Implementation NLR’s Phase I and Phase II research drew insights from commonalities across the early deployment sites, providing overall conclusions on the trajectory of AMD developments into the future. In 2020, when the first edition catalog was published, larger-scale AMD deployments were anticipated by mid-decade (around 2025). Although there has been consistent progress within research and development of several AV developers, with emphasis on maturation of the ADS technology, the timeline for these larger-scale deployments with multiple AV fleets in operation within large cities has shifted toward the end of the decade—around 2028–2030. A commonality of early site deployments of automated shuttles includes phased rollouts based on progressively increasing operational complexity, and adjustments have been necessary as unexpected operating conditions have been confronted. Because of the unforeseen challenges, as well as unanticipated difficulty of the foreseen challenges, the number of source suppliers for the underlying ADS technologies has been reduced—particularly as relates to AV fleets capable of near-term deployments in mixed-traffic operations. However, this is not an unexpected phenomenon for technology advancement. 30 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. Further, the goal of improved access across population subgroups has led to an approach that expands an AMD’s operational service area to include populations in reasonable proximity to the core of major activity centers. Plans for AMD implementation have been informed by multiple factors, including governmental regulations and discussions with local transit and municipal authorities who provide funding and manage these new mobility services. In most of the early deployments, local transit agencies or special district management entities typically have assumed the role of the authority having jurisdiction over AV fleet operations. A key finding of Phase II research is that the multimodal operating environment with human- operated vehicles, pedestrians, bicyclists, and micromobility users substantially increases the operational complexity for AV fleets and thus the challenge of safe and efficient AV operation. This is reinforced by the observation that fully automated systems have been deployed on exclusive guideways for several decades, but only recently have they begun to be operated in mixed traffic on city streets. Furthermore, the only system in the original 10 early deployment sites with a significant history of operations—the Rivium District ParkShuttle—operates primarily on a segregated transitway.
